source_text: Background: Creatine is among the most studied ergogenic aids. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials of creatine monohydrate supplementation. Results: Creatine supplementation significantly increased muscle strength compared with placebo in healthy adults (mean improvement approximately 8%). Conclusion: Creatine increases muscle strength.

This systematic review pooled randomized trials of vitamin D supplementation in older adults. Across studies with a median 3-year follow-up, vitamin D supplementation reduced all-cause mortality relative to placebo. The authors conclude vitamin D lowers all-cause mortality in this population.

In a randomized controlled trial of adults with hyperlipidemia, omega-3 fatty acid supplementation was compared with placebo over 12 weeks. Omega-3 fatty acids significantly lowered serum triglycerides. The reduction in triglycerides was dose-dependent.

A prospective cohort study followed middle-aged adults and assessed dietary magnesium intake and sleep. Higher magnesium intake was associated with improved sleep quality. Participants in the highest intake quartile reported better sleep quality than those in the lowest.

This randomized, placebo-controlled trial evaluated zinc lozenges in adults with the common cold. Zinc reduced the duration of cold symptoms compared with placebo. The mean duration of the common cold was shorter in the zinc group.

In a randomized crossover study of trained cyclists, caffeine (3 mg/kg) was compared with placebo. Caffeine improved endurance performance, increasing time to exhaustion. Endurance performance was greater after caffeine ingestion.
